lines: I've put my spectacles down in the garden and I can't see to find them. You'll appreciate the difficulty.
They'll be by the beans. The garden gate is round the side.
In the garden, by the rows. I'd go myself, but I'd only tread on them.
That's them. Thank you.
Have an apple. Have two. I sit out here and watch the road, and there's nobody on it to give them to.
I stay out here till the bell, then I go in. I don't know who started that. Everybody does it.
You've not seen a bill-hook? Hooked blade, ash handle. I put it down in the clearing and turned round, and it wasn't there.
It'll be there. Things always are, out here. They're just not there while you're looking.
In the clearing. I've looked. It wants a different pair of eyes.
That's it. Where was it?
Stuck in by the point? I don't do that. Take some wood. I cut more than I burn. I cut more every year.
I stop at four. The light goes wrong under the trees after four, like it's coming in from the side.
I've locked myself out, if you can believe it. The spare's under a stone in the garden.
I can't think which stone. I've been standing here since the milk came. It's silly, but I don't like to turn my back on the house.
In the garden. Under a stone. There are a lot of stones.
Oh, that's it. Thank you.
Take these. They were my mother's pansies, and they come up whatever I do to them.
I lock it at nine and I check it at ten. Once I found it open at ten. I'd checked it at nine.
The hens have laid. First time in a week.
Would you fetch them in from the hen house? I'd like them in before anything else has them. There's more about than there was.
The hen house, by the farmhouse. Mind the brown one; she's sat on them.
Three. That's all of them.
Have an apple. I'd give you an egg, but I want to see them all in the one bowl for a day or two.
He went in the barn after his dinner and he hasn't come out.
I won't knock. He doesn't like it. Would you? Say it's only about his tea.
The big doors. Knock twice. Say it's about his tea.
Counting. He'll be counting the sacks.
He's counted them every day since March. There were twelve in March. Take these for your trouble.
He says there's eleven. There should be twelve.
I know where the other is. It's in the sheep pen. He put it there himself on Sunday. Would you fetch it? If I tell him, he'll only start again from one.
In the pen with the sheep. Don't say I told you.
That's twelve. He'll be out now.
Take this. It's from the pantry. It's good, whatever it is. My mother put it up, and she always knew.
He came out for his tea. He sat where he could see the barn door. I didn't ask.
You knock twice and say it is only about his tea.
Inside, a man's voice says he is counting, and he will be out when he has finished, and would you please not knock again.
"Eleven," says the voice behind the door. "Eleven."
The big doors are shut. Inside, somebody is moving sacks about, slowly.
Would you draw me a bucket from the well? My arms aren't what they were.
And taste it, would you? It's tasted of something since March. I'd like somebody young to tell me I'm imagining it.
The well, on the green. Let the bucket right down. The first of it is always warm.
Pennies. Did it taste of pennies?
That's it. That's exactly it. Take a couple of bottles. It's still good water, whatever it tastes of.
I want to know if it's the same next door. I've not asked. We don't, much, since March.
Would you knock? It's the next house along. Don't say it was me wanted to know.
The next house along. Knock, and ask about the water. Don't say it was me.
Since March. They said since March?
Nobody said. Well. I didn't ask. Take these, and thank you. I'll go round myself tomorrow. I will.
I've been round. We had a cup of tea, pennies and all. We didn't talk about it. We talked about the bell, and how it's been going early.
You let the bucket right down and wind it up. The water is clear and very cold.
It smells of pennies. It tastes of them, too.
A stone well with a wooden lid. The bucket is up, and the chain is wet to the top.
You knock. A man answers without opening the door.
"Pennies? Since March. We drink it anyway. Would you not knock after the bell, please. We don't answer after the bell."
Nobody comes. The curtains are drawn, and have been drawn some time; the sun has faded them in stripes.
Somebody knocks at my door after the bell. Most nights now. Three knocks, and when I look there's nobody.
I won't go out after. But the plot's soft; there'd be prints. Would you look, by daylight?
The vegetable plot, past the green. Look in the rows.
A glove? And no prints?
No. Well. Thank you for looking. Take an apple; I don't want you going without something.
I know that glove. I'd rather not say whose.
Would you take it next door and ask? Knock three times. No. Knock twice.
The next house along. Knock twice.
His father's. Yes.
I'll leave a light on in the window. You have this one. It's a good light, and I've others.
Nobody knocked last night. I sat up for it. I'm not sure that's better.
You knock twice. The door opens the width of its chain, and a man takes the glove and looks at it a long time.
"That's my father's," he says. "He went out one night in November, to see who was knocking."
The chain is on. Through the gap you can see a coat on the hook, and a pair of boots under it, very clean.
There's men sit round a fire out at {place:pryor_camp}, off the road. A fire nobody's lit. They've sat there since the winter.
I knew them. We all did. Would you put them down? Gently, if there's a gentle way. I don't want to know how.
{place:pryor_camp}. Off the road. You'll see the fire, and you'll see it isn't lit.
It's done, then.
Don't tell me. Take these. I was keeping them for myself, and I'll not be going anywhere I'd need them.
Their mother still lays the places. I don't go round at teatime.
There's a bag been in the yard since Sunday. A traveller's. Nobody's come for it.
Would you bring it in? I'd sooner not open it myself. I'd sooner somebody else had.
In the yard, past the trough. Canvas, with a strap.
Nothing with a name in it?
A ticket for Sunday's train, not punched. He was here for it, then. He just didn't go. Have something from the kitchen.
He had the back room. He left the key on the barrels round the side, every morning, like I'd not know where to look.
Would you fetch it? I'll let the room. I can't keep a room for a man who sleeps in the yard.
The barrels, round the side. On the one nearest the wall.
Four?
We've three rooms. We've always had three. I'll hang it on the board with the others, and I'll not let it. Take these.
Doors shut at nine. There's been a knock at the back, some nights. I leave the key to four on the board, in case.
On top of the barrel nearest the wall: a room key on a wooden tag. The tag says 4.
An ale barrel, empty by the sound of it. The ring on top has been worn bright by something put down there every day.
I'm three short in the pen. Three sheep don't walk off on their own.
There's a lot camped at {place:hurst_camp}, off the road. Would you go and look? Not to do anything. I want to know for certain first.
{place:hurst_camp}. Keep your distance. Look for fleece; they'll not have had the sense to burn it.
That's my mark on it. That's that, then.
Have an apple. I'll be a minute.
I'd like them moved on. I can't do it, and there's nobody to send for.
I'm sorry to ask it. They weren't always like that. Nobody was.
{place:hurst_camp}, off the road. There's three or four of them. Be careful.
It's quiet out that way?
Then take this. The wife keeps it for the winter. The winter can see to itself.
I've moved the pen nearer the house. They go in at eight now, and I stand with them till nine.
I've lost my ring out of the dish on the sill. There was a crow at the window. It had been there all morning, looking in.
They keep what they take at {place:farrant_camp}, off the road. Would you get it back? Mind them. They don't like being looked at.
{place:farrant_camp}. They keep it all in a box. Don't ask me how a crow comes to have a box.
That's it. That's mine.
Teaspoons? They're not mine. I wouldn't want them now if they were. Have these for your trouble.
I keep the window shut now, and the ring on. I'd rather go without the air.
The post's being left in the yard now, not at the door. There's a letter out there.
Would you bring it in? I don't go out to the yard. It's a long way to the yard, these days.
In the yard. It'll be from my son.
From my son. Let's see.
He says the weather's fine and he'll be home on Sunday. He says that every week. Have an apple.
I've written back. Would you take it to my sister at {place:vosper_sister}, down the road? She keeps them.
She won't open the door. Put it through. She'll know it's me.
{place:vosper_sister}, down the road. Through the door. She won't open it.
She took it? Good.
She keeps them all in a tin, his and mine. Take these.
Would you ask my sister for the tin? All of them, his and mine.
It's time they were read in the right order. I've been reading them in the wrong one.
{place:vosper_sister}. She'll put it out on the step for you.
Thank you. Put it on the table.
Take this. It was his, from the dresser. He'd want it used.
I've read them all now, in order. I know when he stopped writing. I'm still waiting for Sunday. You do, don't you.
You put the letter through the flap. It lands on a mat that sounds thick with others.
From inside, a woman's voice: "Thank you. I'll put it with the rest."
"She wants the tin," says the voice. "Well. It's hers as much as mine."
The door opens a hand's width, and a biscuit tin heavy with paper is put out on the step.
Nobody comes. Inside, somebody is sitting very still, the way you do when you hope a knock will go away.
I grew up at {place:hackett_house}. Off the road, that way. It's walls now.
Would you look inside for me and say what's left? I've not been since. I'm not going.
{place:hackett_house}. Mind the rubble inside.
Marks on the door frame. We did that. Every birthday.
The last one higher than the rest? There's nobody left to be that tall. Take this, and thank you.
My mother kept a tin under the front step. Everything that mattered went in it.
Would you fetch it? I know what's in it. I'd still like it.
Under the front step at {place:hackett_house}. The step's still there. It's all that is.
That's the tin.
There. That's the house, with its roof on. Take this. She'd not mind.
I cut on this side of the road now. I can't see it from here. That's how I like it.
Pencil marks on what is left of the door frame, with names and heights beside them. HACKETT, over and over.
The highest mark is the newest. The pencil has hardly faded.
I've left my scissors in the garden. I was cutting flowers.
Somebody on the road said my name, and I came straight in. There was nobody on the road. Would you fetch them? I'll go out tomorrow.
In the garden, by the rows. I'd left the flowers there too.
Thank you.
In a row? I didn't leave them in a row. Well. Have these. They're from the same bed.
If you hear your name on the road, don't answer it. That's all. I'm not saying anything else.
These are for the woodcutter at {place:venn_wood}. He cuts my wood and he won't take money.
Would you leave them on his woodpile? He won't stop to be thanked. He never does.
{place:venn_wood}. On the woodpile.
Kindling? Tied with green string?
That's my string. I've never given him any string. Well. Have a couple of the apples. I kept the best back.
I went myself yesterday. He was cutting. He didn't look up. I left the string on the woodpile.
You leave the apples on top of the woodpile.
There is a bundle of kindling there already, tied with green string, as if it were waiting to be swapped.
Split logs stacked bark up, more than one man cuts in a week.
There's been a light in {place:denny_ruin} three nights running. Nobody's lived there for years.
Would you look, by daylight, and tell me it's nothing? I'd take it better from somebody who's been.
{place:denny_ruin}. By day, mind. Inside the walls.
Candles. And a chair.
Facing the door. Well, that's somebody who wants to see who comes in. That's all that is. Take this. I'll not sleep either way.
Four nights now. I've started going home the long way round, so I don't pass it.
Candle ends, a great many, burnt right down in saucers along what is left of the wall.
One kitchen chair, facing the doorway, with nothing on it. The seat is clean.
I've potatoes to lift and a back that won't have it.
Would you lift them for me? Before the frost. It comes on the same night every year. I've written it down.
In the garden, the row by the fence. They come up easy this year. Too easy.
That's a good row. That's a very good row.
Bigger than I put them in. Take these from the cupboard instead. I'd rather keep those till I've looked at them properly.
I've looked at them. They're potatoes. I've put them out of the house all the same.
My clock's stopped. It stopped at nine. I went out to see if it was the weather, and I dropped the key.
Would you find it? It's the only clock I have out here. I don't like not knowing when it is.
In the clearing somewhere. A little brass key.
That's it. Thank you.
I'll set it by the light and put it right when the bell goes. You always know nine, out here.
It's kept time since. Except it stops at nine for a moment every night, and then goes on.
The shed door's stuck. Since the weekend. It's never been locked, and it won't open.
Put your shoulder to it, would you? Low down. It sticks at the bottom.
The shed. Shove low down.
Open? Good.
Swept? I don't sweep it. Well. Somebody has. Take this for your shoulder.
I leave the shed door open now. I'd rather see in.
You put your shoulder to the door, low down. It holds, and then gives all at once.
Inside, the floor is swept, everywhere except a square in the middle, the size of a chair.
A plank shed. The floor inside is swept round a square of sawdust the size of a chair.
There's an owl nested in the woodpile. I heard it. I'll not burn a stick of it till I know the nest's empty.
Would you look? My knees won't have the bending.
The woodpile. The gap halfway up. Mind your fingers.
Buttons?
Owls do that. They take things. Have some wood, from the other pile.
I'm burning the other pile first. There's plenty.
A gap halfway up the woodpile, lined with straw. No owl.
In the straw, three buttons: small, brown, a child's, all off the same coat.
My brother cuts at {place:voke_brother}. We've not spoken since Easter.
Would you take him this tea? Leave it by his fire. Don't say it's from me. He'll know.
{place:voke_brother}. By the fire. Don't say anything.
Did he drink it?
No, you'd not know. That's fair. Have these.
There was a can on my step this morning. Empty. Washed.
You leave the can on a stone by the fire. Nobody says anything.
A ring of stones and last night's ash. Two stones are set by it to sit on. One is worn smooth; the other is not.
His tea's ready and he's not come in. He sits out in the garden, evenings.
Would you tell him? Mr Grey. That's his name. It was, when he came.
In the garden. He'll be sat with his cup.
Not there? He'll be walking.
He walks a great deal, now. Take an apple. I'll keep his tea warm. I always do.
He came in at ten. I heard him on the stairs. His door has been locked since June, and I have the only key.
A cup of tea on the path, cold, with a skin on it. Nobody in the garden.
The earth in the rows has been walked, up and back, up and back, in a very straight line.
Would you water the seedlings? I can't carry the can any more.
From the left, mind. My wife always did it from the left. They grow toward where she stood.
In the garden. From the left.
From the left? Good.
They'll do now. Take these. She grew them, and they come up every year without me.
They lean toward the door now. Just to the left of it. That's where she stood.
You water the row from the left, the way he asked.
Every seedling in the garden leans the same way: toward the house, a little to the left of the door.
I lent the family at {place:sayer_house} my ladder in the spring. For the roof.
I don't need it. I'd just like to know it's still there, and still mine. Would you look?
{place:sayer_house}. Off the road. It'll be against the wall. It's got my name on it.
Tarred? They've looked after it.
I'll fetch it Sunday. Take these.
I've not fetched it. They'll want it for the roof.
A ladder against the wall, freshly tarred. On the second rung, in white paint: SAYER.
Under it, in the same paint and a different hand: RETURN BY SUNDAY. There is nothing above it but sky.
They had my husband's good coat off the line. I know who. The lot at {place:rendle_camp}, off the road.
Would you get it back? It's the coat he's to be buried in. He's not ill. It's just the one he's to be buried in.
{place:rendle_camp}. They'll have it in their box. Be careful of them.
That's it. Brushed.
Folded? It's never been folded like that. Take these, with thanks.
He wore it to church on Sunday. He said it fitted better than it used to.
Has the bell been going early for you? It has for me. I'd like to be sure, and I don't stay up for it.
Would you stand in my clearing after nine and listen, and tell me in the morning if it goes twice? There's a chalk mark where to stand.
In the clearing, after nine. Stand on the chalk mark. Listen north, toward the hill.
Twice? I knew it.
I'll set my watch by the second one. Take this. You were out after nine for me.
I set my watch by the second bell now. I'm early for everything. I don't mind.
You stand on the chalk mark and listen north.
The bell goes at nine, from the hill, as it should. It goes again a little after, from somewhere much nearer.
An X in chalk on a flat stone, where somebody wants somebody to stand. It has been chalked over more than once.
There's a stump in the clearing the cutters have put their names in for a hundred years.
Would you read me the newest? My eyes are going. Somebody's cut one since Friday, and nobody's been.
The old stump, in the clearing. The newest is at the bottom.
What did it say?
Read it again. No. There's nobody by that name round here. Take this, anyway.
I've not cut my own name in. I'd have to go under the newest one, and I'd rather not.
Names cut in the stump, one under another, each with its year. The years go back further than the tree could have stood.
The newest is at the bottom, the wood still pale: {name}, and this year.
Take this to the old lady at {place:ruck_cottage}? She's nobody to cut for her.
She'll want to pay you. Don't let her. She's done it thirty years, and I've never once got away.
{place:ruck_cottage}. Leave it at the door.
She paid you, didn't she.
Thirty years. Never once. Have some wood as well, so you're square with somebody.
She told me there was somebody new on the road. I said I'd heard.
The door opens on its chain. A thin hand takes the kindling, and comes back out with a paper bag of grapes.
"For your trouble. No, take it. I've always paid for my wood."
Nobody comes. Inside, somebody is laying a table, one plate at a time.
